```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A tsflow project can be an ordinary analysis folder or an R package. Both use
the same pipeline definitions and can run directly or through targets. The
package framework adds reusable functions, a generated transform registry,
documentation, and tests. Neither packaging nor targets is required to use tsflow.

## Start a package

Install `usethis` and `roxygen2` if needed, and `testthat` to run the generated
tests. The walkthrough uses those packages directly; devtools is optional.

```{r}
tsflow::create_tsflow_package("mypipeline")
```

This creates the package without switching your working directory or opening an
editor. Open the new directory in your editor, or change to it explicitly:

```{r}
setwd("mypipeline")
source("run.R")
result$values$adjusted
```

The starter uses quarterly sample inputs and produces 20, 40, 60, and 80. It
also shows `result$errors` and `result$missing_inputs`: the runner uses
`error_mode = "collect"` so independent series can finish even when another
series fails.

The generated structure is:

```text
mypipeline/
  DESCRIPTION                      # package dependencies and registry roclet
  R/
    example_inputs.R               # replace sample values with your loaders
    scale_series.R                 # tagged example transform
    run_pipeline.R                 # exported direct execution entry point
  inst/
    extdata/
      pipeline.csv                 # series and steps
      pipeline.meta.yml            # shared variables and outputs
    tsflow/
      registry.yml                 # generated; commit with the package
  tests/
    testthat.R
    testthat/test-pipeline.R        # pipeline validation and expected output
  run.R                            # run directly during development
  README.md                        # walkthrough for this package
```

`man/` and `NAMESPACE` are generated during creation. Complete the package's
`DESCRIPTION` with your title, authors, description, and chosen license as you
would for any new R package.

## Replace the example

Start with `R/example_inputs.R`. It returns a named list of raw series; list names
must match the raw names referenced in the CSV. You can read files, call an API,
or accept inputs supplied by the caller. Keep credentials outside your code.

The example CSV is:

```csv
name,input,step_1,step_2
scaled,raw,scale_series(factor = @factor),
adjusted,scaled,,mul(2)
```

Its sidecar defines `factor: 10` under `vars` and requests `adjusted` under
`outputs`. Replace those series, steps, parameters, and outputs with your own.
The CSV and sidecar ship inside the package; `run_pipeline()` finds them with
`system.file()`, so an installed package can run from another working directory.

## Add a transform and its test

```{r}
tsflow::use_tsflow_transform("rebase")
```

This creates `R/rebase.R` and `tests/testthat/test-rebase.R`. The first argument
receives the incoming series; subsequent parameters can be supplied by the CSV.
For example, replace the stub with:

```{r}
#' Rebase a Series
#'
#' @param x An incoming time series.
#' @param base The reference value.
#' @return The series as an index with reference value 100.
#' @tsflow transform
rebase <- function(x, base) {
  x / base * 100
}
```

Update its test to check expected values and preservation of the time index.
Then regenerate the registry and documentation:

```{r}
roxygen2::roxygenise()
testthat::test_local()
```

If you already use devtools, `devtools::document()` and `devtools::test()` perform
the corresponding documentation and testing steps.

The `@tsflow transform` tag registers the function under its own name. Tagged
functions need not be exported; helpers without a tag stay private. The configured
roxygen roclet writes `inst/tsflow/registry.yml`. Regenerate it whenever you add,
rename, or remove a tagged function, and commit it with the code.

You can now use `rebase(base = @base)` in the CSV, adding the shared `base`
parameter to the sidecar. Update the starter pipeline test as its expected output
changes.

The registry can also be used explicitly:

```{r}
pkgload::load_all()
registry <- tsflow::package_registry("mypipeline")
plan <- tsflow::plan_pipeline(
  "inst/extdata/pipeline.csv", transforms = registry$transforms
)
```

After installing the package, callers can run it directly:

```{r}
mypipeline::run_pipeline()
mypipeline::run_pipeline(inputs = my_inputs)
```

## Add another pipeline

Use the scaffolding helper to add a named pipeline to the same package:

```{r}
tsflow::use_tsflow_pipeline("forecasting")
# Or choose YAML for a different pipeline:
tsflow::use_tsflow_pipeline("sources", format = "yaml")
```

CSV creates `inst/extdata/forecasting.csv` and `forecasting.meta.yml`; YAML
creates `inst/extdata/sources.yml` with its parameters and outputs in that file.
Each also gets a validation test under `tests/testthat/`, using the package's
transform registry. The starter takes an input named `raw` and multiplies it
by a shared `factor` of 10. Replace those steps with your calculation and extend
the test with expected values.

Existing files are protected, including another format or sidecar with the same
name. Adding a pipeline does not change the default runner or `_targets.R`.
Select its path when running it:

```{r}
mypipeline::run_pipeline(path = "inst/extdata/forecasting.csv")
```

From an ordinary project's root, the same helper puts the pipeline files there
and does not add package tests. Supply the selected path to
`tsflow::execute_pipeline()` or `tsflow::tar_tsflow()`.

## Use targets when you want it

Include targets at creation time, or enable it later:

```{r}
tsflow::create_tsflow_package("anotherpipeline", targets = TRUE)
# Or, from the existing mypipeline root:
tsflow::use_tsflow(targets = TRUE)
```

Install `targets` before running the generated `_targets.R`:

```{r}
targets::tar_make()
targets::tar_read(adjusted)
```

The script calls `tar_tsflow()` with the same CSV, registry, and input function.
Direct execution remains available. Existing starter files are preserved, so
enabling targets later does not reset your pipeline or overwrite your code. If
you already have `_targets.R`, add the pipeline to its existing target list by
hand. The package starter's structure is:

```{r}
library(targets)
pkgload::load_all()
registry <- tsflow::package_registry("mypipeline")

list(
  tar_target(tsflow_inputs, example_inputs()),
  tsflow::tar_tsflow(
    "inst/extdata/pipeline.csv",
    transforms = registry$transforms,
    hooks = registry$hooks
  )
)
```

For real input files, track their paths with `targets::tar_target(...,
format = "file")` and load those tracked files in a downstream target. External
inputs hidden inside a function are not automatically monitored by targets.
See `vignette("targets", package = "tsflow")` for input tracking and caching.

Package versions are recorded for registered package functions. During
`pkgload::load_all()` development, changing only an internal helper without
bumping the package version can leave stale targets. Invalidate affected targets
before rerunning; package-code fingerprinting is a planned follow-up.

## Start without a package

```{r}
tsflow::use_tsflow("myanalysis")
# Or include targets immediately:
tsflow::use_tsflow("myanalysis", targets = TRUE)
```

An ordinary project puts `pipeline.csv` and `pipeline.meta.yml` at its root, with
supporting functions under `R/`. Run `source("run.R")` from that root. Functions
are sourced and registered explicitly; no `DESCRIPTION`, registry roclet, or
package installation is required.

Add your own functions to `R/`, then source and register them in `run.R` and, if
used, `_targets.R`. The same pipeline format and runtime APIs apply. To move to
a package, create a package scaffold and move the pipeline into `inst/extdata/`
and the functions into `R/`, tagging the transforms you wish to register.

## Advanced: evaluation hooks

Most pipeline packages need only transforms. If a pipeline author chooses when
an operation applies, it is a transform; rules that must hold across evaluations
of a particular kind can use hooks. See
[Writing pipeline packages: advanced hooks](package-hooks.html)
(`vignette("package-hooks", package = "tsflow")`) for the hook contracts,
registry setup, and an executable provenance-preservation example.
